t.3.15.1: While the great-souled Rāghava was dwelling there happily, with the passing of autumn the welcome season of winter set in.
t.3.15.2: Once, when the night had given way to dawn, Raghunandana went to the lovely river Godāvarī for his ritual bath.
t.3.15.3: Following behind him and Sītā, the valiant brother Saumitri, humbly bowing and with a water-pot in his hand, spoke these words.
t.3.15.4: This is that season, so dear to you, O sweet-spoken one, now arrived, by which the auspicious year shines forth as if adorned.
t.3.15.5: The world is harsh with frost, the earth is garlanded with crops, the waters are unfit for enjoyment, and fire, the bearer of oblations, is pleasing.
t.3.15.6: Having worshipped the ancestors and the gods with offerings of the new harvest's first fruits, good people who have performed the āgrayaṇa rite at its proper time are freed from their sins.
t.3.15.7: The country regions abound in things to be desired and are richer still in milk and its products, and kings eager for conquest move about for the sake of their campaigns.
t.3.15.8: While the sun steadfastly attends the southern quarter frequented by Antaka, the northern quarter does not shine, like a woman bereft of her tilaka.
t.3.15.9: Rich, of its very nature, in stores of snow, and now with the sun far away, the mountain Himavān is plainly true to its name: Himavān, the snowy one.
t.3.15.10: The days are now exceedingly pleasant for moving about, and at midday they are pleasant to the touch; in them the sun is welcome, while shade and water have become unwelcome.
t.3.15.11: The days now appear with a gentle sun, laden with mist, keenly cold and windy, the forests deserted and everything blighted by frost.
t.3.15.12: Now the nights pass by, nights in which sleeping under the open sky has ceased, led by the constellation Puṣya, ruddy-grey with frost, cold, and grown ever longer in their span.
t.3.15.13: The moon, its charm passed over to the sun, its disc reddened by the frost, does not shine, like a mirror dimmed by breath.
t.3.15.14: Moonlight dimmed by frost does not shine even on the night of the full moon; like Sītā darkened by the heat of the sun, it is seen but does not look beautiful.
t.3.15.15: Cool to the touch by its very nature, and now pierced through with frost, the western wind blows, doubly cold in this season.
t.3.15.16: The forest tracts, veiled in mist and rich with barley and wheat, shine forth when the sun has risen, alive with the calls of krauñcas and sārasas.
t.3.15.17: The rice plants, golden in their lustre, shine forth, drooping slightly with their heads full of grain and shaped like the flowers of the date palm.
t.3.15.18: Though it has risen far into the sky, the sun, its approaching rays veiled by cold mist and frost, looks like the moon.
t.3.15.19: The sunshine, whose strength cannot be felt in the forenoon and which is pleasant to the touch at midday, shines upon the earth faintly reddish and somewhat pale.
t.3.15.20: The ground of the forests, its green grass somewhat moistened by the falling of the frost, shines with the young sunlight settled upon it.
t.3.15.21: Bound in the darkness of hoarfrost and veiled by the gloom of mist, the flowerless rows of forest trees appear as if fast asleep.
t.3.15.22: Now the rivers shine with their waters veiled in mist, their sārasa cranes known only by their cries, and their banks of sand wet with frost.
t.3.15.23: Because of the falling of frost, the mildness of the sun, and the cold, even the water lying on the mountain peaks is, for the most part, sweet to the taste.
t.3.15.24: With their leaves withered by age, and their filaments and seed-cups shrivelled, the lotus ponds, ravaged by frost and left with only their stalks, no longer shine.
t.3.15.25: But at this very time, O tiger among men, the righteous-souled Bharata, filled with sorrow, is practising austerities in the city out of devotion to you.
t.3.15.26: Having given up the kingdom, honour, and many pleasures of various kinds, he lives as an ascetic, restrained in his food, and lies upon the cold surface of the earth.
t.3.15.27: He too, surely, at this very hour, intent on his ritual bath and attended always by his subjects, goes forth to the river Sarayū.
t.3.15.28: Raised in the utmost comfort, delicate and afflicted by the cold, how indeed does he plunge into the Sarayū in the last hours of the night?
t.3.15.29: With eyes like lotus petals, dark-complexioned, glorious, slender-waisted and great, he knows dharma, speaks the truth, is restrained by modesty, and has conquered his senses.
t.3.15.30: Speaking pleasantly and sweet of nature, the long-armed subduer of foes, having renounced manifold enjoyments, has taken refuge with his noble elder brother with his whole being.
t.3.15.31: Heaven has been won by your brother, the great-souled Bharata, who follows your example in asceticism even while you dwell in the forest.
t.3.15.32: “Men follow not their father's nature but their mother's”: this well-known popular saying has been proven otherwise by Bharata.
t.3.15.33: She whose husband is Daśaratha and whose son is the virtuous Bharata, how could that mother Kaikeyī be of such a cruel outlook?
t.3.15.34: As the righteous Lakṣmaṇa was speaking these words thus out of affection, Rāghava, unable to bear that censure of their mother, spoke.
t.3.15.35: Dear brother, you must never in any way find fault with our middle mother. Speak only of that same matter, of Bharata, the lord of the Ikṣvākus.
t.3.15.36: Though my mind is firmly resolved upon dwelling in the forest and steadfast in its vow, yet, burning with affection for Bharata, it is made foolish once again.
t.3.15.37: Lamenting thus, Kākutstha reached the river Godāvarī there and, together with his younger brother and with Sītā, performed his ritual bath.
t.3.15.38: Then, having satisfied the ancestors and the deities with offerings of water, they, with minds composed, praised the risen sun and the gods.
t.3.15.39: Having bathed, Rāma, with Sītā as his companion and together with Lakṣmaṇa, shone forth like the blessed Rudra, lord of the daughter of the king of mountains, when he has bathed with Nandin at his side.
